pages: FICTIONAL HEARING — Harbor inspection dispute. January 8, 2026. Judge Vale: This is a scheduling hearing only. City counsel Reed: The engineer is unavailable this week; we request a short continuance. Owner counsel Moss: No objection if the existing access restriction remains. Judge Vale: The matter is continued to February 12. The existing access restriction remains unchanged. No merits ruling is made today.

positions.text: City counsel requested a brief continuance because the engineer was unavailable; owner counsel did not object provided the existing access restriction continued.

orders.text: The court continued the matter to February 12, leaving the existing access restriction unchanged and making no merits ruling.

pages: FICTIONAL HEARING — Harbor inspection dispute. February 12, 2026. Judge Vale: We address temporary inspection access, not ownership or final repair liability. City counsel Reed: We seek limited inspection access to the drainage channel. The engineer observed water rising after the last storm, but could not inspect the covered culvert. The photographs show standing water, not the cause of blockage. We request a supervised dye test, not excavation. We cannot accept a restriction to exterior photographs because those will not identify where water enters the covered section. We propose a weekday inspection with city insurance and advance notice. Owner counsel Moss: We oppose an unrestricted entry order, not all inspection. The old survey excludes the east strip, and ownership of that strip remains disputed. Equipment must not cross the disputed strip without an agreed route. The tenant stores temperature-sensitive supplies near the channel; a shutdown could spoil them. We need written test limits and restoration duties, not an informal promise to be careful. We dispute the engineer's claim that our gate prevented inspection: the request arrived after the crew had left, and a representative offered another date. No witness has established who caused the blockage. Tenant counsel Lane: The tenant supports a safe inspection but requests protected delivery hours and no business closure. The morning loading period is essential. Advance notice must reach the tenant directly, not only the owner. If testing interferes with refrigeration, supplies must be moved first at the city's expense. Utility counsel Hart: The utility takes no position on ownership. Its cable lies near the proposed entry route. We request cable location before testing, no powered excavation, and a utility observer with authority to stop work if a marked cable is threatened. City counsel Reed: We accept a utility observer and a marked route, but an unrestricted stop-work right could defeat even safe testing. The engineer should decide whether the dye test itself presents a risk. Owner counsel Moss: A city employee should not have final authority over a disputed safety issue. An independent engineer should resolve that question before the operation resumes.

FICTIONAL HEARING CONTINUED. Engineer Rowan, sworn: I saw water standing near the channel on January 20. I did not enter the covered culvert. The photographs cannot establish causation. A dye test may identify a flow path; it cannot by itself establish who caused a blockage or who must pay. I cannot rule out a downstream obstruction. Hand-carried equipment should suffice for the proposed test. I have not verified the cable depth. The test could interrupt power if the cable is damaged, but proper marking reduces that risk. I recommend daylight work with a utility observer. Owner counsel Moss: The independent surveyor's letter concerns the east boundary, not channel capacity. We offer it solely to explain the route dispute, not as an expert drainage opinion. Tenant counsel Lane: The delivery log records a normal loading period of 7 to 10 a.m.; it does not establish that every delivery occurred then. The tenant cannot identify the blockage's cause. Utility counsel Hart: The utility map is approximate, not a field location. No one should rely on it as an excavation clearance. City counsel Reed: We request a decision today because another storm is forecast, but acknowledge the forecast does not prove an imminent failure. Owner counsel Moss: We request postponement until ownership is tried. If the court allows access now, the order must expressly reserve title and liability and prohibit using temporary access as an admission. Judge Vale: I admit the photographs and delivery log for their limited purposes. I receive the survey letter only to explain the route dispute, not to decide title. The utility map requires field verification. There is evidence supporting a limited inspection, but no finding of fault or imminent collapse. The engineer's testimony does not establish causation. Waiting for a title trial would delay a useful inspection; a supervised test can proceed while reserving title and liability. I reject both unrestricted city access and complete postponement.

FICTIONAL HEARING — RULINGS CONTINUED. Judge Vale: The city may conduct one supervised dye test after these conditions are met. The parties must approve a marked route that avoids the disputed east strip; if no route is agreed, access does not begin and the parties return for directions. The city must give five business days' written notice to both owner and tenant, identifying the test, personnel, insurer, route, and expected duration. Work is limited to daylight hours after 10 a.m. and must not close the tenant's business. No powered excavation is authorized. The utility must mark the cable in the field before any equipment enters, and a utility observer must attend. The observer may stop work for an identified cable risk, stating the reason in writing. A disagreement about that risk goes to an independent engineer jointly selected by city and utility; the city engineer has no unilateral right to resume. Refrigeration must remain operating; if a planned interruption becomes necessary, the tenant's supplies must first be relocated at city expense. An unplanned interruption requires immediate cessation and protective measures, not continued testing. The city must restore disturbed surfaces within two business days and provide dated photographs to owner and tenant. The city must preserve raw test results and share them with all parties within three business days; no party may describe the temporary test as a determination of fault. Title, causation, permanent repairs and allocation of costs remain reserved. This is permission for inspection, not a repair order. Counsel must confer on the route and independent engineer within seven days. A status hearing is set for March 5 at 9 a.m. If the conditions cannot be met, the city must seek further directions rather than treating the order as unconditional access. City counsel Reed: We understand. Owner counsel Moss: The reservation of title and liability is important to our agreement on the procedure. Tenant counsel Lane: We understand the no-closure condition. Utility counsel Hart: We understand the limited stop-work authority. Judge Vale: Those acknowledgments do not waive any party's reserved position.

positions.text: The city sought limited access for a supervised dye test rather than excavation, because exterior photographs would not reveal the covered culvert's flow path. It cited rising water after a storm, acknowledged photographs did not establish the blockage's cause, proposed weekday work with insurance and notice, and opposed confining the inspection to exterior photographs. The owner opposed unrestricted entry rather than every inspection. It disputed ownership of the east strip and wanted equipment to avoid it, challenged the claim that its gate had prevented inspection because the request came after the crew left and another date was offered, and requested written test limits and restoration duties. It sought postponement until title was tried; if access went ahead, it demanded an express reservation of title and liability and no inference of an admission from temporary access. The tenant supported safe inspection but sought protected delivery hours, direct notice and no business closure. It stressed refrigeration for temperature-sensitive supplies and requested relocation at city expense before any planned power interruption. The utility took no position on ownership, but requested field cable location, no powered excavation and a utility observer able to stop work if a marked cable was threatened. The city accepted a marked route and observer but resisted unrestricted stop-work authority and wanted its engineer to assess testing risks. The owner opposed unilateral city control of a disputed safety decision and sought independent engineering review before resumption. The city sought a ruling because another storm was forecast, while acknowledging that the forecast did not establish imminent failure. The owner emphasized that nobody had established who caused the blockage. At the conclusion, counsel acknowledged the inspection procedure, with the owner emphasizing the title/liability reservation, the tenant the no-closure condition, and the utility the limited stop-work authority; the court clarified that acknowledgment did not waive reserved positions.

evidence.text: Sworn engineer Rowan saw standing water January 20 but did not enter the culvert. The photographs could not establish causation; a dye test might identify a flow path but would not establish who caused a blockage or who must pay, and a downstream obstruction remained possible. Hand-carried equipment should suffice; cable depth was unverified. Rowan recommended daylight work with a utility observer. The survey letter addressed the route boundary, not drainage expertise. The delivery log described a normal 7–10 a.m. loading period, not the time of every delivery. The utility map was approximate and required field location, not an excavation clearance.

orders.text: The court allowed a conditional supervised inspection, rejecting unrestricted access and complete postponement. It admitted photographs and the delivery log for limited purposes, received the survey letter only to explain the route dispute, and required field verification of the utility map. It found support for inspection but not fault or imminent collapse; title and liability remained unresolved. Only one supervised dye test was authorized. Before entry, parties must agree to a marked route avoiding the east strip; absent agreement they must return for directions. The city must give both owner and tenant five business days' written notice specifying the test, personnel, insurer, route and expected duration. Work must occur in daylight after 10 a.m., without business closure or powered excavation. Field cable marking and a utility observer are required before equipment enters. The observer may stop work for an identified cable risk and must state reasons in writing; disputes go to an independent engineer jointly selected by city and utility, with no unilateral city-engineer resumption. Refrigeration must remain operating. Before a planned interruption, supplies must be relocated at city expense; an unplanned interruption requires immediate cessation and protective measures. Disturbed surfaces must be restored within two business days, with dated photographs sent to owner and tenant. Raw results must be preserved and shared with every party within three business days. The test determines neither fault nor permanent repairs or costs; it is permission to inspect, not a repair order. Counsel must confer on the route and independent engineer within seven days. A March 5 status hearing is set for 9 a.m. If conditions cannot be met, further directions are required rather than unconditional entry. Counsel's acknowledgments waived no reserved positions.

pages: FICTIONAL CITY REPORT — January 22, 2026. The January 8 hearing continued the dispute without changing the access restriction. On January 20 engineer Rowan photographed standing water near the channel but did not enter the covered culvert. The photographs do not establish causation. The east boundary remains disputed. The city recommends a supervised dye test with advance notice and insurance, not excavation or a finding of owner fault. A storm is forecast, but imminent failure has not been established. The tenant requests uninterrupted refrigeration and protected loading hours. The utility requests field cable marking. No new access order has yet been made.

pages: FICTIONAL CITY REPORT — March 2, 2026. Background: the January 8 continuance left access restricted; engineer Rowan photographed standing water January 20 without inspecting the culvert. The photographs did not establish causation. At the February 12 hearing, the court authorized one supervised dye test, conditioned on route agreement, direct notice, cable marking and business protection, reserving title and fault. New developments: on February 19 city and owner agreed to a route avoiding the east strip. The utility marked the cable February 24. A test planned for February 27 did not proceed because the independent engineer was unavailable; no entry occurred. The tenant reported that refrigeration remained operating, but no inspection result exists. The city proposes March 9 for testing subject to renewed compliant notice and observer availability; this is a proposal, not a court-ordered testing date. The March 5 status hearing remains set. The city still recommends inspection, not excavation, and requests no change to reserved title or fault issues.
